title: Krishna Guides Arjuna Against Ashvatthama's Brahmastra
one_line_summary: After Ashvatthama releases the Brahmashira weapon at the Pandavas, a terrified Arjuna calls on Krishna, who tells him only a brahmastra can counter it; Arjuna discharges it and, at Krishna's word, withdraws both blazing weapons to save the worlds.
source_excerpt: When the blazing weapon flares in every direction, Arjuna cries out, 'Krishna, Krishna, mighty-armed one, giver of fearlessness to your devotees, you alone are the rescue of those being burned.' Krishna answers: 'Know this to be the brahma weapon of Drona's son. He does not know how to recall it. Only an astra can quell an astra.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 21, 26-27)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Krishna's Verdict on Ashvatthama
one_line_summary: When Ashvatthama, the murderer of the sleeping children, is dragged before Krishna and the Pandavas, Krishna urges that the brahmin-slayer must be punished but not slain, and pronounces the compromise Arjuna carries out: strip his jewel and shave his head, sparing his life.
source_excerpt: Krishna says: 'A brahmin's unworthy son is not to be slain, yet an assailant deserves punishment — both are my ordinances; uphold them. Keep the promise you made to your beloved, and satisfy Bhima, Panchali and me.' Then Arjuna, understanding Krishna's heart, cut off the jewel along with the hair of the brahmin, released him from his bonds, and drove him from the camp. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 52-55)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering.

title: Krishna Shields Parikshit in Uttara's Womb
one_line_summary: As Krishna departs Hastinapura, the terrified Uttara cries for protection from Ashvatthama's weapon; Krishna enters her womb by his yoga-maya and shields the unborn Parikshit with the Sudarshana disc, extinguishing the unerring Brahmashira.
source_excerpt: Uttara cries: 'Protect me, protect me, great yogin, Lord of gods, master of the world! May this blazing iron-tipped arrow burn me, but let my embryo not fall.' The Lord, loving to his devotees, understood that Drona's son's weapon was aimed to leave the Pandavas without heir; the Lord, indwelling soul of all beings, covered the womb of Virata's daughter with his own maya to preserve the Kuru line. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 8-13)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering.

title: Kunti's Farewell Hymn to Krishna
one_line_summary: As Krishna prepares to leave Hastinapura for Dwaraka, Queen Kunti offers a parting eulogy recalling how he saved her family from poison, fire, exile and weapons, and asks only that his remembrance ever bind her; Krishna smiles and grants her prayer.
source_excerpt: Freed from the brahma weapon, Kunti addressed Krishna as he turned to depart: 'I bow to you, the primal Person... You freed Devaki and me, with my sons, again and again from danger — from poison, from the great fire, from the cruel assembly, from the hardships of forest exile, from the weapons of great chariot-warriors.' And the Lord, whose every glory she had praised, smiled gently. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 16-17, 22, 43)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering.

title: Bhishma's Passing in Krishna's Presence
one_line_summary: Lying on his bed of arrows at the auspicious northern solstice, Bhishma fixes his gaze on Krishna standing before him, glorifies him as Narayana himself, and passes away with his mind merged in the Lord, while the sages and Pandavas look on.
source_excerpt: Bhishma says: 'This very Krishna, who came to me as I give up my life, out of love for his unalloyed devotees — may he be my refuge.' Then, gathering in his speech, he fixed his unblinking gaze upon the four-armed Krishna standing before him in yellow robes, and offered his final praise: 'May my love rest on Krishna...' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 21, 29-31)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering.

title: Krishna Departs Hastinapura for Dwaraka
one_line_summary: After restoring Yudhishthira to the throne and staying some months to comfort his relatives, Krishna takes leave of the grieving Pandavas and women of Hastinapura and sets out for Dwaraka, journeying through many kingdoms.
source_excerpt: Having stayed in Hastinapura some months to gladden his friends and please his sister, Hari took his leave, embraced and bowed to all, and mounted his chariot; Subhadra, Draupadi, Kunti, Gandhari, Dhritarashtra and the others could not bear the separation, their eyes fixed on him as he departed. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 6-12)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering.

title: Krishna's Homecoming to Dwaraka
one_line_summary: Krishna reaches his own prosperous realm of Anarta, sounds his conch, and is welcomed by the joyful citizens, his father Vasudeva, Balarama, Ugrasena and his queens, who receive him with offerings and embrace.
source_excerpt: Approaching his own prosperous land of Anarta, Krishna blew his conch to dispel his people's sorrow; hearing it, the citizens rushed to see their lord. Vasudeva, Akrura, Ugrasena and the wondrous Rama, with Pradyumna and others, came forth on chariots to meet him; entering his father's house, Krishna bowed to his seven mothers led by Devaki, who lifted him to their laps and bathed him with tears of joy. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 1-2, 16-18, 28-29)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering.

title: Arjuna Brings News of the Yadava End
one_line_summary: Arjuna returns from Dwaraka broken and weeping and tells Yudhishthira how the Yadavas, deluded by a brahmin's curse and drunk on wine, slew one another with their fists, and how Krishna then departed the earth, after which the Kali age set in.
source_excerpt: Arjuna, his heart hollowed by grief, tells the king: 'In the city of our friends, the Yadavas, deluded by the curse of the brahmins, drinking the madira wine and beside themselves, slew one another with their bare fists; but four or five were left.' And Suta adds: when Mukunda abandoned this earth, in that very moment the Kali age, the cause of all evil for the unawakened, entered. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 21-22, 35)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering.

title: The Sages Curse Samba and the Iron Mace Appears
one_line_summary: Yadu boys dress Samba as a pregnant woman and ask the visiting sages what 'she' will bear; the angered sages curse that he will bring forth an iron mace to destroy the clan, and the mace appears, is ground and cast into the sea, and its remaining iron, swallowed by a fish, later becomes the hunter's arrow.
source_excerpt: Disguising Samba as a woman, the boys asked the sages: 'This dark-eyed one is pregnant; what will she give birth to?' The angry sages answered: 'She will bear an iron mace, the destroyer of your clan.' Samba brought forth the mace; the Yadava king had it ground and cast into the sea, and a fish swallowed the last bit of iron, which in the hunter's hands became the arrow. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 13-15, 20-22)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Brahma and the Gods Urge Krishna to Return to His Abode
one_line_summary: After one hundred and twenty-five years, Brahma and the assembled gods come to Dwaraka, praise Krishna, and remind him that the earth's burden is lifted and his clan is nearly consumed by the curse, asking him to return to his own abode.
source_excerpt: Brahma said: 'A hundred and twenty-five years have passed since you descended in the Yadu line. Your work for the gods is all but done, and this clan is nearly destroyed by the brahmins' curse. If you think fit, return to your supreme abode.' Krishna answered that the earth's burden was indeed lifted and he would go at the end of the curse. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 24-30)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Uddhava Begs Krishna Not to Leave Him Behind
one_line_summary: Seeing the fearful omens in Dwaraka and Krishna's intention to depart, Uddhava falls at his feet and pleads that he cannot bear to be separated even for a moment and begs to be taken along; Krishna, granting his wish, begins to instruct him.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Lord, even for half a moment I cannot bear to leave your lotus feet; carry me also to your abode.' Krishna, addressed by his devoted servant, answered: 'What you have said is exactly my own intent; Brahma, Shiva and the world-guardians long for my return to heaven.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 41-42, 49-50)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Yadu Meets the Wandering Avadhuta
one_line_summary: King Yadu meets a serene, fearless brahmin avadhuta and, astonished at his freedom, asks how he attained such wisdom; the avadhuta answers that he has twenty-four gurus from whom he drew his understanding.
source_excerpt: Yadu asked the wandering brahmin: 'You act like a child, a madman, a ghost, and yet you are a sage; how did you gain such wisdom?' The brahmin answered: 'I have many gurus, O king — earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon, sun, the pigeon, the python, the ocean, the moth, the bee, the elephant, the honey-gatherer, the deer, the fish, Pingala, the osprey, the child, the maiden, the arrow-maker, the serpent, the spider and the wasp — twenty-four in all.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 26-34)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Avadhuta's Lessons from the Elements
one_line_summary: The avadhuta relates what he learned from the earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon and sun: forbearance, detachment, unaffectedness, purity, untaintedness, waxing and waning, and the one soul reflected in many bodies.
source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'Though trampled by all beings, the wise one does not stray from his path — this I learned from the earth. Moving among the objects of sense, the yogi remains unattached like the wind; pure and sweet like water; untainted by what he consumes, like fire; waxing and waning like the moon; one soul appearing in many bodies, like the sun.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 36-50)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Pigeon and the Hunter's Net
one_line_summary: A pigeon so bound to his mate and chicks that when a hunter's net traps his family he casts himself into the same net and perishes with them, teaching Krishna's hearers that clinging to home and family destroys.
source_excerpt: The pigeon, seeing his chicks and his mate caught in the hunter's net, lamented: 'Alas, my poor mind! My home is destroyed; of what use is my life now?' And he too flew into the net, and the cruel hunter took them all. 'Thus the householder who feeds his family like a bird, attached and without peace, comes to ruin.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 66-72)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Python's Contentment and the Ocean's Depth
one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the python to accept whatever food chance brings without striving, and from the ocean to remain deep, full and unmoved whether rivers pour in or not.
source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'The python eats whatever comes by chance, whether fine or foul, much or little, and lies still for days without food if nothing comes. The sage is serene and unfathomable like the ocean, which neither swells when rivers pour in nor dries when they do not.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 1-5)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Moth and the Bee
one_line_summary: From the moth, which perishes in the flame, the avadhuta learns that desire for a woman's beauty destroys; from the bee he learns to take only the essence from many flowers without storing anything up.
source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'Bewitched by a woman's beauty, the uncontrolled man falls into blinding darkness like the moth into the flame. And the sage gathers the essence from great and small teachings, like the bee from flowers, but stores nothing for tomorrow.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 6-9)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Elephant, the Honey-Gatherer, the Deer and the Fish
one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the elephant, ensnared by lust for the decoy she-elephant, from the honey-gatherer, whose hoard others enjoy, from the deer, snared while listening to music, and from the fish, hooked through the tongue, how the senses lead one to ruin.
source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'The ascetic should not touch a woman even of wood, lest he be bound like the elephant caught by the she-elephant; the wealth painfully hoarded is enjoyed by others, as the honey-gatherer steals the bees' honey; the deer is snared by song; and the fish, allured by the tongue's bait, meets death on the hook.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 12-18)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Pingala the Courtesan's Renunciation
one_line_summary: The courtesan Pingala, waiting through the night for a client who never comes, is seized with disgust at her own longing, renounces it, and sleeps in peace, teaching that hope is the worst of pains and despair the highest joy.
source_excerpt: Pingala said: 'Look at the extent of my delusion! I sought a lover for gain, when the giver of all joy is ever near. What I sought so wretchedly, let me give up.' Cutting off her hope of a lover, Pingala sat down and slept in peace: 'Hope is the greatest of pains; freedom from hope is the greatest of joys.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 30, 42-43)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Osprey, the Child, the Maiden and the Arrow-Maker
one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the osprey (letting go of prey seized by stronger birds), the child (freedom from care), the maiden (solitude — she broke her bangles one by one to stop their clinking), and the arrow-maker (one-pointed concentration).
source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'A maiden, alone, husking grain, heard her bangles clink and broke them one by one until only one remained, and it was silent — so the sage should dwell alone. And like the arrow-maker so absorbed in straightening his shaft that he did not see the king pass by, the mind should be fixed on one point.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 4-12)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Serpent, the Spider and the Wasp
one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the serpent (dwelling in another's abandoned hole, homeless), from the spider (who spins the web from himself and withdraws it again), and from the wasp (who becomes what it meditates upon).
source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'Building a house brings only sorrow — the serpent enters another's abandoned home and thrives. As the spider sends forth the thread from its own heart, plays with it and draws it back, so the Lord creates, sustains and withdraws the world. And as the wasp, meditating on its captor, becomes like it, so the mind becomes what it dwells upon.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 14, 20-22)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Swan Teaches the Kumaras
one_line_summary: Asked by his disciples about the swan form, Krishna recounts how Brahma's sons Sanaka and the others, unable to get an answer from Brahma, were taught by Krishna himself appearing as a swan (hamsa), who resolved their doubt.
source_excerpt: Krishna said: 'The mind-born sons of Brahma asked him the subtle goal of yoga; pondering their question, Brahma meditated on me, and I appeared to them in the form of a swan. They asked who I was, and I answered that if in truth there is no difference in the self, their very question has no ground — know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 15-23)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Miserly Brahmin of Avanti
one_line_summary: A wealthy but miserly brahmin of Avanti, spurned by his own relatives and stripped of his wealth, is seized with dispassion, becomes a wandering mendicant, and, enduring the mockery and blows of the crowd, sings the song of the mendicant: the mind alone is the cause of joy and sorrow.
source_excerpt: The brahmin of Avanti, once wealthy, miserly and cruel, saw his wealth taken by relatives and thieves; dispassion arose, and he became a silent, wandering mendicant. Though people seized his staff, mocked and struck him, he sang: 'Neither people, nor gods, nor fate are the cause of my joy and sorrow — it is the mind alone that turns the wheel of existence.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 5-11, 41)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Pururava's Lament for Urvashi
one_line_summary: King Pururava (Aila), mad with grief when the nymph Urvashi leaves him, pursues her naked and weeping; realizing his delusion, he sings the song of Aila on the futility of attachment to women, and attains peace.
source_excerpt: King Aila sang: 'Alas, what delusion has seized me! A monarch, I became a plaything of a woman; I, who was emperor, followed her like a beast, naked and weeping. What is this foul body of flesh and bone, and what these charms imputed to it? So let no wise man cling to women.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 6-21)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Krishna Sends Uddhava to Badari
one_line_summary: Krishna commands Uddhava to leave for his hermitage at Badarikashrama and abide in the teaching he has received; the grief-stricken Uddhava circumambulates him, places his feet upon his own head, and departs bearing Krishna's sandals.
source_excerpt: Krishna said: 'Go, Uddhava, as I have commanded, to my hermitage called Badari; there, dwelling on what I have taught, you will come to me beyond the three paths.' Uddhava, unable to leave him, walked around him again and again, placed Krishna's feet on his head, and, bearing his sandals, at last went forth. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 40-45)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Krishna Directs the Yadavas to Prabhasa
one_line_summary: Seeing the terrible omens rising in Dwaraka, Krishna tells the Yadava elders to leave at once for the holy tirtha of Prabhasa, and they cross the sea in boats and chariots to worship there.
source_excerpt: Krishna said: 'These dreadful omens are the banners of death; not for a moment should we remain here. Let the women, children and elders go to Shankhoddhara, and let us go to Prabhasa where the Sarasvati flows westward.' The Yadava elders answered 'so be it' and crossed over to Prabhasa. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 4-9)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Yadava Fratricide at Prabhasa
one_line_summary: Drunk on maireya wine at Prabhasa, the Yadavas, deluded by Krishna's maya and the brahmins' curse, fall upon one another, and when their weapons fail they seize the eraka reeds — which have become iron clubs — and annihilate one another; Balarama then yields up his body in yoga.
source_excerpt: Drinking the maireya wine, their minds overthrown, the proud heroes fell upon one another — Pradyumna against Samba, Akrura against Bhoja, Aniruddha against Satyaki; fathers against sons, kinsmen against kinsmen. When their arrows were spent, they seized the eraka reeds, which had become like iron clubs, and with them slew one another. Then Balarama, entering yoga at the ocean's shore, gave up his mortal frame. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 11-20, 25)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Hunter Jara Shoots Krishna's Foot
one_line_summary: After the Yadavas' destruction, Krishna sits in meditation at the foot of a pippala tree; the hunter Jara, mistaking Krishna's foot for a deer's, shoots it with the arrow made from the mace's iron, then, seeing the four-armed Lord, falls at his feet in terror.
locations: at the foot of a pippala tree
source_excerpt: Seated at the foot of a pippala tree, four-armed and radiant, Krishna placed his right foot upon his thigh; the hunter Jara, taking the foot for a deer's face, pierced it with the arrow fashioned from the mace's iron. Seeing the four-armed Lord, the terrified hunter fell at his feet, begging forgiveness. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 26, 31-34)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Krishna's Last Message to Daruka
one_line_summary: Krishna consoles the hunter, granting him heaven, and when his charioteer Daruka weeps at his feet, sends him to Dwaraka with the final message: the Yadavas are destroyed, Balarama is gone, and the sea will swallow Dwaraka, so let the people follow Arjuna to Indraprastha.
source_excerpt: Krishna said to Jara: 'Fear not; rise. This was my own doing. Go, with my leave, to the abode of the virtuous.' And to his charioteer he said: 'Go to Dwaraka and tell my kinsmen of the destruction and of Balarama's departure and of my state. The sea will soon flood the city I have left; let all of you, with Arjuna's help, go to Indraprastha.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 38-39, 45-47)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Krishna's Final Departure
one_line_summary: As Brahma, Shiva and the hosts of gods watch, Krishna, seeing Brahma before him, closes his lotus eyes, draws his opulences into himself, consumes his body with the fire of yoga, and enters his own abode, his path unfathomable even to the gods.
source_excerpt: Brahma, Shiva, Indra, the sages and the hosts of gods came, eager to see the Lord's departure, raining flowers and singing his deeds. Krishna, seeing Brahma, gathered his opulences into himself, closed his lotus eyes, consumed his body with the fire of yoga, and entered his own abode, while the gods, amazed, could not trace his path. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 1-8)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: The Sea Swallows Dwaraka
one_line_summary: After Krishna's departure, his queens and family ascend the funeral pyres, Arjuna performs the last rites, and the sea floods and swallows Dwaraka — all but the Lord's own dwelling; Arjuna leads the survivors to Indraprastha and installs Vajra.
source_excerpt: Daruka told Vasudeva and Ugrasena of the destruction; Devaki, Rohini and Vasudeva, seeing neither Krishna nor Balarama, gave up their lives in grief, and the queens, led by Rukmini, entered the fire. The sea swallowed Dwaraka, all but the Lord's own abode; and Arjuna, leading the surviving women, children and elders to Indraprastha, installed Vajra as king. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 14-24)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition).

title: Vidura Meets the Grieving Uddhava
one_line_summary: On the banks of the Yamuna, Vidura meets Uddhava, who is plunged in grief and remembrance of Krishna's departure, and hears him lament that the Yadavas never recognized the Lord who dwelt among them.
source_excerpt: Uddhava, asked by Vidura, was for a moment silent, sunk in the nectar of Krishna's feet, his limbs thrilling with devotion; then, wiping his eyes, he smiled and said: 'The sun Krishna has set; what good news can I tell in homes bereft of fortune? Wretched is this world, and more so the Yadavas, who dwelt with Hari and knew him not.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 3-7)
notes: Frame unit: the Vidura-Uddhava conversation that recounts the pastimes below. Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Putana's Poisoned Milk
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how the demoness Putana (Baki), who offered Krishna her poison-smeared breast to kill him, was instead granted the goal of a nurse — death at his hands became her liberation.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Alas! The wicked Putana, who with murderous intent gave him her breast of deadly poison, attained the goal of a nurse. To what other compassionate one could we turn for refuge?' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 22)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna's Birth and Removal to Nanda's Vraja
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls that Krishna was born of Vasudeva and Devaki in Bhoja's prison to relieve the earth's burden, and was carried by his father, fearing Kamsa, to Nanda's Vraja, where he lived hidden for eleven years with Balarama.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Born of Vasudeva and Devaki in the prison of the Bhoja king, the Lord, prayed to by the earth, came to relieve her. Then, carried by his father in fear of Kamsa, he dwelt in Nanda's Vraja for eleven years with Balarama, his glory concealed.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 24-25)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna's Cowherd Childhood and the Demons of Kamsa
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls Krishna's childhood in Vraja — herding calves and cows with the cowherd boys on the Yamuna, playing the flute — and how he playfully defeated the shape-shifting demons Kamsa sent against him.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Surrounded by the calves, he herded them and sported in the Yamuna's groves, showing the cowherds his enchanting childhood play, weeping and laughing with a lion-cub's glance; playing the flute, he delighted the cowherds — and the shape-shifting demons sent by the Bhoja king he dispelled in sport, like toys.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 26-29)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Subdues Kaliya the Serpent
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how Krishna, when the cows were poisoned by the Yamuna's venom, subdued the serpent-king Kaliya, raised them up, and restored the water to its natural purity.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'The cows, perishing from drinking the poisoned water, he restored; subduing the king of serpents, he raised them up and made that water again fit to drink.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 30)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Lifts Govardhana to Shield Vraja from Indra
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how, when the proud Indra poured down rain in fury upon Vraja, Krishna sheltered the terrified cowherds beneath the umbrella of Govardhana hill, granting them his grace.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'He had the cowherd king perform the go-savana sacrifice; and when Indra, his pride broken, rained down in fury, the terrified Vraja was sheltered by the umbrella of the hill, the Lord favouring his devotees.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 31-32)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: The Autumn Rasa Dance
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how, in the clear autumn moonlight, Krishna sang and sported as the ornament of the circle of the cowherd women of Vraja.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Honouring the face of night washed by the rays of the autumn moon, he sang sweet songs and sported as the ornament of the circle of the women.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 33)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Slays Kamsa
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how Krishna, coming to the city of his parents with Balarama, hurled Kamsa, the leader of the enemy hosts, from his high seat and dragged him lifeless upon the ground.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Then, coming to the city of his parents with Balarama to free them, he hurled the leader of the enemy hosts from the high seat and dragged him lifeless upon the earth.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 34)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Restores Sandipani's Son
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how Krishna, having studied the Vedas once through from his guru Sandipani, restored the guru's dead son to him as a gift, bringing him back from the realm of death.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Having studied the whole Veda once through from Sandipani, he granted his guru the boon of his dead son, bringing him back from the belly of Pancajana.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Carries Off Rukmini and Wins Satya
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how Krishna carried off Rukmini, Bhishmaka's daughter, by the gandharva rite, and how he defeated the proud kings to win Satya (Nagnajiti) at her svayamvara.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Summoned by Bhishmaka's daughter, he carried off his own share by the gandharva rite while the suitors looked on; and, humbling the proud kings, he won Nagnajiti at her svayamvara.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 2-3)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Fetches the Parijata Tree
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how Krishna, wishing to please his beloved like a common man, went for the celestial Parijata tree, and how Indra, blind with rage, attacked him with his host.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Wishing, like a common man, to please his beloved, the Lord went for the celestial tree; the thunderbolt-wielder, blind with rage, rushed at him with his host, as if he were a plaything of the women.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 4)
notes: The Parijata episode (not in the canonical arc list). Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Slays Narakasura and Weds the Sixteen Thousand
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how Krishna slew the demon Naraka (Bhauma), who had seized the earth's princesses, and how the freed princesses chose Krishna as their husband, who married them all in one moment and begot sons in each.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Seeing the son of the earth-goddess who devoured the heavens, he slew him; the princesses seized by Bhauma, seeing Hari the friend of the distressed, rose and chose him, and he took their hands in one moment in their many houses, begetting ten sons in each.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 5-8)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Defeats the Besieging Kings and Demons
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how Krishna destroyed the hosts of Kala, Magadha (Jarasandha) and Shalva that besieged Dwaraka, and slew Shambara, Dvivida, Bana, Mura, Balvala, Dantavakra and others.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'The hosts of Kala, Magadha and Shalva that besieged the city he slew; Shambara, Dvivida, Bana, Mura and Balvala, and others like Dantavakra, he killed, or had killed.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 9-10)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: The Kurukshetra War
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how the earth shook at Kurukshetra as the armies of the warring cousins gathered, and how Duryodhana lay at the last with his thigh broken, the burden of the earth lifted by Krishna's design.
themes: the lifting of the earth's burden
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'The earth trembled at Kurukshetra beneath the armies of the kings who fell on either side; and Suyodhana, with his followers, lying with his thigh broken, he did not rejoice to see.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 11-12)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna Foresees the Yadavas' Self-Destruction
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls Krishna's deliberation that the Yadu warriors, themselves the remaining burden of the earth, could be destroyed in no other way than by their own quarrel, and that when he acted, they would destroy themselves.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'What burden of the earth remained, when Drona, Bhishma, Arjuna and Bhima were gone, but the unbearable host of the Yadavas? When they quarrel among themselves, eyes red with wine, there is no other way to destroy them; when I act, they will vanish of themselves.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 13-14)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: The Sages Curse the Yadu Boys
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how, angered by the Yadu and Bhoja boys at their play in the city, the sages pronounced the curse that sealed the clan's destruction.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Once, in the city, the sages, angered by the Yadu and Bhoja boys at their play, pronounced a curse — knowing the mind of the Lord.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 23)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: The Yadavas Journey to Prabhasa
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how, some months after the curse, the Vrishnis, Bhojas and Andhakas, deluded by fate, joyfully journeyed to the tirtha of Prabhasa, bathed, and gave rich gifts to the brahmins.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Then, after some months, the Vrishnis, Bhojas and Andhakas went joyfully to Prabhasa, deluded by fate; there they bathed, honoured the gods and rishis, and gave the brahmins cows, gold, silver, beds, garments, chariots, elephants and lands.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 24-27)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: The Yadavas Destroy Each Other
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how the Yadavas, their minds deranged by the maireya wine, fell upon one another at sunset and were crushed like reeds, destroying their own clan.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Their minds deranged by the fault of the maireya wine, at sunset there was among them a crushing of one another, like reeds.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Krishna's Final Instruction to Uddhava
one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how, as the Yadavas destroyed themselves, Krishna sat at the foot of an ashvattha tree and, finding Uddhava there, granted him the ancient teaching and the supreme state, commanding him to go to Badari.
locations: at the foot of an ashvattha tree
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'The Lord, seeing that course of his own maya, sipped the Sarasvati and sat at the foot of a tree; he said to me, go to Badari. Yet, unable to leave his feet, I followed; and he, finding me there, told me: I know your heart's desire; I grant you what is hard for others to attain. And he taught me the supreme state.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 2-10, 18)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.

title: Uddhava Departs for Badarikashrama
one_line_summary: Having received the supreme teaching from Krishna, Uddhava bows and departs, heart-torn, to the hermitage of Badarikashrama, there to worship Hari in meditation, as Vidura hears the account and weeps.
source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'So, having worshipped his feet and received the path of self-knowledge, I bowed to the Lord and came away, heart-torn with separation; I will go to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and Nara performed their long austerities.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 19-21)
notes: Verse numbers per the GRETIL file's internal numbering (offset by one from the standard critical edition). Retrospective unit: recounted by Uddhava to Vidura.
